data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["SRC_008 concerns calibration curves specifically; this claim generalizes to any within-evaluation metric","SRC_008's limitation is about measurement granularity; this claim is about identifiability of causal structure from observational data"],"overturn_conditions":["Demonstration that at least one observable within a single evaluation has different expected values under the two hypotheses","Proof that error covariance structure is not jointly compatible with both causal reliability and coincidental tracking","An argument that the problem's 'single evaluation' permits structural assumptions that render the hypotheses identifiable"],"shared_structure":["Single evaluation cannot distinguish calibration from coincidence because both hypotheses predict the same observations","The problem's constraint mirrors the limitation that calibration curves across difficulty levels cannot be computed when outcomes are binary within a single evaluation"],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_008"],"transfer_claims":["Any single-evaluation metric is consistent with both genuine reliability and coincidental tracking","The distinction requires either a second evaluation or ex-ante knowledge of the checklist's causal mechanism","The problem's demand is analogous to asking whether a single coin flip can distinguish a fair coin from a biased coin that happens to produce heads on this flip"]},"claim":"The distinction between genuine reliability gain and mere checklist compliance that happens to track the right answer cannot be made within a single evaluation, because compliance and reliability are observationally equivalent when outcomes are the only ground truth. The problem's demand for a single-evaluation discriminator is formally unsatisfiable: any metric computed within one evaluation (including error covariance, calibration, or item-level analysis) is consistent with both hypotheses.","counterconditions":[{"case":"A single evaluation contains sufficient information to distinguish causal reliability from coincidental tracking (which would require an argument that the two hypotheses have disjoint likelihoods given any possible observation)","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The problem permits implicit use of distributional assumptions about the evaluation set that would allow inference from a single sample","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The distinction can be made via internal consistency metrics alone, without any out-of-sample validation","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Within a single evaluation, every observable\u2014accuracy, agreement, error patterns, calibration\u2014is compatible with two generative models: (1) the checklist causally produces reliability by enabling effective aggregation of independent errors, or (2) the checklist is a proxy that correlates with the answer on this particular evaluation set but does not produce generalizable reliability. Without a second evaluation on a different distribution or holdout set, these hypotheses cannot be distinguished. The problem's constraint to a single evaluation removes the primary tool for distinguishing reliability from coincidence. This is a structural limitation, not a measurement problem: the information needed to separate the hypotheses is not present in the data.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
